checkpoints: sns.Publish() returning a successful MessageId only confirms SNS received the message and started the fan-out process — it does NOT confirm any specific subscriber actually received it, so "publish always succeeds" is fully consistent with one subscriber getting nothing.

This is a silent failure by design: when SNS's delivery to a subscriber is rejected (e.g. for lacking permission), it has no way to report that error back to the code that called Publish(), since the MessageId was already returned before SNS even started the fan-out — the publisher can never observe a per-subscriber delivery failure this way.

The Terraform root cause: only ONE aws_sqs_queue_policy resource exists, attached to the inventory queue; the email queue has no corresponding policy at all — which is exactly why inventory keeps receiving messages while email doesn't, even though both subscribe to the same topic.

SQS by default does not allow an external service (including SNS) to send messages into a queue unless an explicit aws_sqs_queue_policy grants sqs:SendMessage to the sns.amazonaws.com principal — so without that policy, the email queue silently rejects every message SNS tries to deliver.
Fix (core grant): add a separate aws_sqs_queue_policy for aws_sqs_queue.email, structured like inventory's — Principal = sns.amazonaws.com, Resource = the email queue's ARN.

Fix (scope it): the policy's Condition.ArnEquals["aws:SourceArn"] must point to the exact ARN of the order_created topic — without it, any other SNS topic in the account could also gain permission to write into this queue (confused-deputy risk), not just the intended one.

Verify by publishing a test message and calling receive-message separately on each queue — don't just trust the returned MessageId, since it never confirmed per-subscriber delivery in the first place.
Also watch the SNS topic's NumberOfNotificationsFailed metric going forward, to catch any remaining or future unauthorized-subscriber delivery failure early, rather than discovering it manually.

Vi phạm nguyên tắc cốt lõi của DynamoDB single-table design: chỉ tạo GSI cho access pattern đã được validate, không tạo speculative — trong 4 GSI chỉ có GSI1-status là hợp lệ (gắn với access pattern thật là dashboard filter theo status), còn GSI2-email, GSI3-city, GSI4-category được thêm "phòng khi cần" mà không có query/access pattern thực tế nào đang dùng.

Hậu quả chi phí ghi (write cost) là cụ thể và tức thời chứ không phải rủi ro tương lai: mỗi GSI biến một lần ghi vào base table thành chi phí GẤP ĐÔI vì DynamoDB phải ghi base table VÀ đồng bộ ghi vào từng GSI chứa attribute liên quan; với 3 GSI dư thừa, mỗi lần create/update order phải trả thêm 3 lần chi phí ghi mà không mang lại giá trị truy vấn nào.

projection_type = "ALL" trên cả 4 GSI khiến MỌI attribute của base table bị copy vào từng GSI, nhân đôi chi phí lưu trữ thêm một lần nữa cho mỗi index; với 3 GSI dư thừa dùng ALL, storage bị lãng phí nhiều lần so với việc chỉ dùng KEYS_ONLY hoặc INCLUDE với vài attribute thực sự cần cho access pattern đó (mà ở đây thậm chí access pattern còn không tồn tại).

Điểm mấu chốt dễ bị bỏ qua: DynamoDB không bao giờ cảnh báo "GSI này chưa từng được query", nên khoản lãng phí ghi + lưu trữ từ 3 GSI thừa tích lũy âm thầm mỗi tháng, chỉ lộ ra khi có người soi kỹ hóa đơn — bản chất nguy hiểm nằm ở tính silent/khó phát hiện, không chỉ ở con số cộng dồn.

Đề xuất fix: xóa ngay GSI2-email, GSI3-city, GSI4-category — vì GSI có thể được thêm vào bất cứ lúc nào sau này (khác với LSI phải tạo ngay lúc tạo bảng), nên không có lý do gì để thêm chúng một cách speculative từ đầu.

Khi access pattern thật sự xuất hiện (ví dụ có yêu cầu nghiệp vụ cụ thể cần tra cứu order theo customer email), lúc đó mới tạo GSI tương ứng, và nên cân nhắc dùng projection_type = "INCLUDE" chỉ với vài attribute mà pattern đó cần, thay vì mặc định ALL cho mọi GSI.
The root cause is using `Scan` with a `FilterExpression` instead of `Query`, for an access pattern that Query can fully serve.

`Scan` reads the ENTIRE table before applying the filter, so its cost is based on the size of the whole table (roughly table_size / 4KB RCU) rather than the number of items returned — for this 100GB table that works out to roughly 25 million RCU per scan, even though only a handful of orders actually satisfy the PENDING + over-30-minutes condition.
That cost is multiplied by frequency: the Lambda repeats this scan every 5 minutes, 24/7 (~288 times a day) — this is what's driving the DynamoDB bill spike.
Independent of frequency, each single run still has to read all 100GB before it can filter, which is inherently slow — this is why the Lambda keeps timing out.
The fix is to create a new GSI with `status` as hash key and a time field like `createdAt` as range key (or similar field supporting range comparisons).

Rewrite the code as a `Query` against that GSI with a `KeyConditionExpression` such as `#s = :pending AND createdAt < :cutoff`, so DynamoDB reads only items matching status and time condition instead of the whole table, making cost proportional to the number of matching items.

To confirm the improvement, compare `ConsumedCapacity` between the old Scan and new Query for the same run (millions of RCU down to tens/hundreds) and watch DynamoDB CloudWatch billing before/after to confirm the cost drop.
Rule scope: `filter { prefix = "backups/" }` limits the lifecycle rule to objects under the `backups/` prefix only, without touching the rest of the bucket.
`transition { days = 30, storage_class = "STANDARD_IA" }` satisfies requirement (1): moves objects to Standard-IA 30 days after creation.

`transition { days = 90, storage_class = "GLACIER" }` satisfies requirement (2): moves objects further to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days — AWS applies multiple `transition` blocks automatically in increasing day order, no manual sequencing needed.
`expiration { days = 365 }` satisfies requirement (3): it fully deletes the CURRENT version of the object 365 days after creation.

Explains the versioning problem behind requirement (4): since the bucket has versioning enabled, every new backup overwriting the object (same key) creates a NEW version and turns the previous one into "noncurrent" — but that old version is NOT automatically deleted, it still exists and consumes storage.
The `expiration`/`transition` fields only apply to the CURRENT version, so they do not handle cleanup of old/noncurrent versions — a separate mechanism is required.

`noncurrent_version_expiration { noncurrent_days = 60 }` satisfies requirement (4): it means exactly "60 days after this version BECAME noncurrent," not 60 days after the object was originally created.

States the general principle for versioned buckets: `transition`/`expiration` govern the current version while `noncurrent_version_transition`/`noncurrent_version_expiration` govern old versions — omitting the noncurrent pair is a common cause of versioned buckets silently ballooning in storage over time.

Requirement (c) (independent delivery to both teams) is solved with the SNS → SQS fan-out pattern: publish the "payment processed" event to an SNS topic, with each team subscribing its own separate SQS queue.

A separate SQS behind SNS for each team (rather than letting teams subscribe directly) is necessary because SNS only pushes messages and doesn't store them — if a consumer temporarily dies or falls behind, the message is lost — whereas a dedicated SQS per team acts as a durable buffer with independent DLQ and retry, so one team's incident doesn't affect the other.

Requirement (b) (correct ordering within the same order) requires both SQS queues to be FIFO (`.fifo`) rather than Standard, since Standard only offers best-effort (approximate, not guaranteed) ordering while FIFO guarantees ordered delivery within the same MessageGroupId.

MessageGroupId should be set to the actual orderId — not a single fixed value shared by every message — so that messages within the same order (charge → refund) stay strictly ordered while different orders can still be processed in parallel.

Requirement (a) (no duplicate processing) is partially handled by FIFO's exactly-once deduplication mechanism (MessageDeduplicationId or content_based_deduplication), but this only works within a 5-minute window.

Because deduplication alone doesn't cover cases outside that window (e.g. client retries, network issues), the consumer itself must be idempotent — e.g., checking whether a paymentId has already been processed via an idempotency-key table before executing the actual charge/refund.

The trade-off to accept is that FIFO caps throughput at roughly 300 msg/s (or 3000 with batching), far below Standard's near-unlimited throughput — but for a payment system, correctness (no duplicates, correct order) matters more than extreme throughput, so the trade-off is reasonable as long as actual traffic doesn't exceed FIFO's limit.
Verdict: attaching only an identity policy on the role in account B is NOT enough to grant cross-account read access to the S3 bucket in account A.

An identity-based policy attaches to a principal (user/group/role) and defines "what this principal CAN DO" — it has no visibility into whether a resource in a different account consents to being accessed.

Cross-account access requires a resource-based policy — here, the bucket policy placed on the S3 bucket in account A — attached to the resource itself and answering "WHO may touch this resource"; only a resource-based policy can name a principal from another account in its Principal block, something an identity-based policy can never do.

AWS applies a "two-key model" for cross-account access: the bucket policy in account A must name account B's specific role ARN in its Principal block, AND that role in account B must still carry its own identity policy allowing s3:GetObject.

Missing either key still results in AccessDenied — this differs from the same-account case, where a resource-policy allow OR an identity-policy allow alone is sufficient; in cross-account, neither one alone suffices, both are required together.
The most common mistake is carrying same-account "either policy is enough" reasoning into a cross-account scenario and forgetting to configure the other side.
Concrete account-A step: create an aws_s3_bucket_policy on the bucket with Principal set to account B's role ARN (optionally tightened with a condition like aws:SourceIp).

Concrete account-B step: attach an aws_iam_role_policy or aws_iam_policy to that role granting s3:GetObject scoped to the exact bucket ARN in account A — the request only succeeds once both sides exist together.

`sts:AssumeRole` mechanism: the principal (the CI pipeline) calls STS, STS checks the target role's trust policy, then returns temporary credentials so the principal acts under that role's identity — effectively becoming that role.
This trust-policy-based permission only governs who may become the target role; it says nothing about handing that role to an AWS service to use on the caller's behalf.

The pipeline's actual situation is different: it doesn't need to become the instance-profile role, it's just attaching that role to a newly launched EC2 instance so the EC2 runs under it, while the pipeline keeps its own identity throughout.

Handing a role to an AWS service to use on its behalf (EC2 with an instance profile, Lambda with an execution role, an ECS task with a task role) requires a separate permission, `iam:PassRole`, which lives in the identity policy of the principal performing the action (e.g. `RunInstances`) and has nothing to do with the STS AssumeRole flow.

Granting the pipeline `sts:AssumeRole` only lets it change its own identity if needed — it does not allow it to attach any role to EC2 — which is why `terraform apply` still gets `AccessDenied` despite already having `sts:AssumeRole`.
The fix is to also grant the pipeline `iam:PassRole`.

That `iam:PassRole` grant must be scoped down: the `Resource` should be exactly the ARN of the role being passed (never `Resource: "*"`), since an unscoped resource would let the pipeline pass any role, including an admin role, to a service — a privilege-escalation path.
The grant should also include a condition `iam:PassedToService = ec2.amazonaws.com` so the role can only be passed to the EC2 service and not abused to pass it to some other unintended service.
Request FAILS (is denied) — the outcome does not change even though the engineer's IAM policy is AdministratorAccess granting full permission in every region.
SCP (Service Control Policy) does not grant permission; it sets the maximum permission CEILING that any IAM policy in the account can reach, applied at the organizational level.
Effective permission is computed by INTERSECTION (AND) of what IAM allows and what SCP does not forbid — not by IAM alone.

Applying that intersection here: AdministratorAccess allows every region, but the OU's SCP allow-list permits only us-east-1, so the intersection is just us-east-1; ap-southeast-1 falls outside it and gets blocked.

The same denial holds even if the engineer is the root user of prod-account, because SCP binds the root user of a member account — unlike Permissions Boundary, a different mechanism (attached at account level to a specific IAM user/role) that does NOT bind root; this root-binding gap is the key SCP-vs-Permissions-Boundary distinction.
Because SCP still binds root, it is the only defense layer that remains effective if a member account's root access key leaks — an attacker with root still cannot exceed the SCP ceiling.

Exception: SCP does not apply to the organization's management account — if prod-account were itself the management account rather than a member account under an OU, the SCP would not apply, and the same ap-southeast-1 EC2 creation request would PASS under AdministratorAccess.
This is exactly why best practice mandates never running workloads in the management account — only in member accounts under an OU, where SCP guardrails actually take effect.
Root cause: the trust policy's condition only pins the `aud` claim (`token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud = sts.amazonaws.com`) and has no condition at all on the `sub` claim.

The `aud` claim alone is insufficient to gate access because it only confirms the token is meant for AWS STS, not who issued it — every GitHub Actions repo in the world configured for OIDC toward AWS produces this same `aud` value, so any repo (including an unrelated intern's personal demo repo) satisfies the only condition present and can successfully assume the role.

The missing claim is `sub`, which for GitHub Actions encodes the specific origin as `repo:org/repo:environment:<env>` (when the workflow runs in a GitHub Environment) or `repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/<branch>` (by branch) — this is the claim that actually distinguishes exactly which repo/branch/environment is calling AssumeRole.
The fix is to add a `StringEquals` condition on `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub` with an exact value scoped to the intended repo (e.g. `repo:my-org/my-repo:environment:production`).
The condition must use `StringEquals`, not `StringLike` with a broad wildcard, since a broad wildcard on `sub` would reopen the same vulnerability by matching unintended repos/branches.

Pinning by `environment:` is preferable to pinning by branch ref, because a GitHub Environment can carry a manual approval gate as an extra protection layer before the workflow reaches the assume-role step.

Verify the fix by running the workflow from a different, non-whitelisted repo and confirming `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` is clearly rejected, while the correct production repo/environment's workflow still assumes successfully as before.

Root cause: iam:CreateRole, iam:AttachRolePolicy, iam:PutRolePolicy, and iam:PassRole are all granted on Resource:"*" in both the permissions boundary and the developer's identity policy — this is the classic privilege-escalation permission combo.

iam:CreateRole has no Condition forcing new roles to be created with the permissions_boundary attached, so the boundary does NOT automatically extend to a role the developer creates — the developer can create a brand-new role with no boundary at all.
Attack step: the developer can then use iam:AttachRolePolicy to attach AdministratorAccess directly to that newly created, unconstrained role.
Attack completes: iam:PassRole open on Resource:"*" lets the developer pass that new admin role to an EC2 instance or Lambda function and execute code there with full admin permissions.

Independent/compounding issue: even if CreateRole is fixed to force a boundary, iam:PassRole on Resource:"*" remains a separate vulnerability — it lets the developer pass ANY already-existing role (including a pre-existing admin role created for other purposes) to EC2/Lambda without needing to create a new role.
Fix for CreateRole: add a Condition (StringEquals on iam:PermissionsBoundary = the developer_boundary ARN) so every role the developer creates is forced to inherit that exact boundary.

Fix for PassRole — narrow Resource: restrict Resource to the specific ARN range/naming convention the developer is allowed to pass (e.g. arn:aws:iam::*:role/developer-*), instead of leaving it as "*".

Fix for PassRole — restrict PassedToService: add a Condition restricting iam:PassedToService to only the needed services (ec2.amazonaws.com, lambda.amazonaws.com), so the passed role can't be attached to arbitrary AWS services.
